title: Loosen an M10 nylon-insert locknut with an adjustable wrench: roll the jaw snug onto the flats, then turn
instruction: Roll the adjustable wrench's thumbwheel until its jaw is snug on the nut's flats, loosen the nut at least 60 degrees counterclockwise with it, and let go of the wrench, leaving it on the nut.
context: An adjustable wrench has to be sized to the nut before it is used: its knurled thumbwheel is rolled with a fingertip until the jaw closes on the flats. A jaw left wider than the nut's corners swings round it; a jaw left loose turns a light nut but bears on its corners, which rounds them or slips under load. General maintenance and repair workers (O*NET 49-9071.00, about 1.5 million in the US, BLS OEWS), electricians (about 0.8 million) and automotive technicians (about 0.7 million) set and use adjustable wrenches every day, among them on nylon-insert locknuts (DIN 985) that resist turning all the way off. Here the jaw starts open 23 mm round an M10 locknut: a fingertip rolls the thumbwheel about two turns until the jaw is snug, then the nut is turned one flat against its nylon insert, and the wrench is let go on the loosened nut.
setup: Station bench; positions in m from the midpoint between the arm bases (left y +0.305, right y -0.305), +x away from the arms, +y left, z up; angles in degrees counter-clockwise from +x seen from above. Both arms at ready. One fixed layout (object_jitter 0); nothing depends on the seed. A painted 330 x 340 x 8 mm steel plate centred at (0.250, -0.050) holds an ISO 4017 M10 x 25 screw (8.8) standing up through a tapped hole at (0.280, 0.060), 17 mm above the plate. On the plate round the screw: a DIN 9021 M10 washer (30 x 2.5 mm), and on it a fresh DIN 985 M10 nylon-insert locknut for every trial (steel 8, zinc plated, 17 mm across flats; listing: Würth 368.10 'M10-1.5 MC NYLON LOCKNUT CLASS 8.8 ZN DIN985'; not ISO 10511, whose M10 is 16 mm across flats) run down with a wrench until it touches the washer, not tightened, with a paint mark across its top and the washer. A Bahco 8071 adjustable wrench (205 mm, 255 g), its jaw set to 23 mm on its scale, lies round the nut with its fixed jaw flat against one flat and the nut against the throat: head on the washer, handle at 210 deg (back and to the right), its end on the plate.
scoring: Snug on the nut (every level): the jaw reads at most 17.5 mm on the wrench's scale with the nut seated between the jaws: its axis inside the jaw opening, each jaw face within 0.5 mm of the flat facing it, the head at the nut's height (the jaws on at least 3 mm of the flats); the top photo and trial video show the wrench sitting on the nut, and a 0.5 mm feeler gauge does not pass between either jaw and its flat. A jaw closed away from the nut is not snug. Whole-trial 0 if the nut is turned clockwise (tightened) past 10 deg (paint mark, trial video). At the end: 1.0 if the nut is loosened at least 60 deg counterclockwise (one flat past its paint mark), the jaw is snug on the nut and was set at most 17.5 mm as the turn began, the wrench lies flat (within 15 deg) on the plate, both grippers are at least 30 mm from wrench and nut, and wrench and nut have stayed still for 1.0 s (trial video; 1 mm and 0.5 deg in the simulator). 0.5 if the nut is loosened 60 deg with the jaw snug on the nut and set at most 17.5 mm as the turn began, the rest not met (a hand still on the wrench, the handle held up). 0.25 if the jaw is snug on the nut with the nut turned less than 60 deg, or the nut is loosened 60 deg with a loose jaw (set over 17.5 mm as the turn began, or not snug on the nut at the end; the setting is read as the nut first passes 10 deg: on the video, with the head covered, a loose pull shows as a free swing of the handle before the paint mark moves, 12.4 deg at 18.4 mm against 3.7 at 17.5 mm). 0 otherwise (an open jaw swings round the nut; a jaw closed away from the nut).
run_limit: 1,800 steps (90 s at 20 Hz): the reference run takes 49.5 s; the rest is room for a learned policy
reset_notes: Run the used nut off the screw with the wrench and set it aside; run a fresh DIN 985 M10 nut down with the wrench until it just touches the washer (do not tighten), paint its mark in line with the washer's, set the jaw to 23 mm on the wrench's scale, and lay the wrench round the nut with its handle at 210 deg (back and to the right) as in the start photo, its fixed jaw flat against one flat (head on the washer, handle end on the plate). A fresh nut every trial keeps the prevailing torque at its first-removal value (ISO 2320: at least 1.5 N m), the same in every trial. About 2 minutes.
fidelity: The task ends at the loosened nut with the wrench left on it (the simulator cannot slide a snug jaw off the hex without dragging it). Nut on a hinge against 1.5 N m (ISO 2320), turned only through the jaws. Stand-ins: knurl 0.5 mm proud of the head; nut 0.25 kg, jaw 80 g; jaw friction 1.0 (dry steel 0.2). On the nut is read from the poses (each jaw face to the nut's outline); the solver's overlap of a face into a flat, at most 0.18 mm in the runs, counts within the 0.5 mm.
